title: Foundations to Athletic: a one-year programme, then continuation cycles
tagline: Muscle and shape first, fat loss alongside, then fitness, power and skill, for a man who has never trained and trains alone.
timelineNote: Phase 4 then repeats in 12-week cycles; Maintenance mode is used only for busy or disrupted periods, and Away mode only for time without a gym
overview:
**What this is.** A structured programme in five phases. It is designed around your priorities (aesthetics, hypertrophy, fat loss, then strength, endurance and VO₂max, then agility, coordination, flexibility, balance and mobility), your schedule (waking 12:00, training about 13:00, work 16:00–01:00), solo training in a well-equipped gym, and the evidence on how untrained people adapt.

**The shape of the year.**

| Phase | Weeks | Training | Main aim |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 · Orientation | 1 | 2 light technique sessions, a baseline test day, 1 easy aerobic | Learn the gym, measure your starting point, calibrate nutrition |
| 1 · Foundations | 12 | 3 full-body sessions + 2 aerobic | Technique, first muscle and strength, slow fat loss |
| 2 · Development | 16 | 4 upper/lower sessions + intervals + run–walk | More volume for priority muscles, barbell lifts, VO₂max, a running base |
| 3 · Athletic | 24 | 4 upper/lower + intervals + long session; plyometrics and agility in warm-ups | Hypertrophy block, strength-and-power block, physique-and-conditioning block |
| 4 · Continuation | 12, repeating | Same structure, your choice of emphasis | Keep progressing or hold your shape |

**How it works day to day.** Every session has three parts: a warm-up, the main training and a cool-down with stretching. Sessions are designed to fit roughly 60–65 minutes so you can eat and get ready before work. Loads are never prescribed as fixed kilograms; you find your own and progress them with [[rule:double-progression|double progression]], judging effort in [[term:rir|repetitions in reserve]]. Fat loss is driven by a modest energy deficit and verified by your waist and weight trends, not by the scale's body-fat number.

**What you log elsewhere.** In your workout app: exercise, load, reps and an effort rating (RPE) for every working set, plus short notes. On your scale or in the [[tool:checkin|check-in tool]]: morning body weight. With the tape: waist every week, all girths and photos every four.

**When you cannot get to the gym.** Two optional modes protect your progress when the full programme is not possible; you switch to either from Today, and the app remembers your week and brings you back to it. [[phase:pm|Maintenance mode]] is for busy or disrupted weeks when a gym is available: two short full-body sessions and two short aerobic sessions. [[phase:pa|Away mode]] is for trips, holidays, family visits or a closed gym, with no machines or weights: three full-body bodyweight sessions and two aerobic sessions a week, made harder by changing the exercise (leverage, range, tempo, one leg or a loaded backpack) rather than by adding weight, with sets ending close to failure ([[rule:away]]).
outcomes:
These are **population averages and ranges from research in untrained adults**, not predictions for you. Individual responses vary several-fold [@Hubal2005_variability; @Ahtiainen2016_heterogeneity], and part of the apparent variation is measurement error [@Dankel2019_trueVariability]. Use them to calibrate expectations, then trust your own trend data after about 8–12 weeks.

| Horizon | Strength | Muscle | Fat and waist | Aerobic fitness | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| End of Phase 1 (≈3 months) | Working loads on most lifts +20–50% (inference from typical novice progress; largely neural and skill learning early) [@Skarabot2021_neural_review] | About +1.5 kg lean mass per ~10 weeks on average [@Benito2020_wholeBodyHypertrophy]; individual range roughly 0 to >3 kg (inference) | Depends on the deficit; see the nutrition plan | VO₂max rises within weeks; supervised training adds about 5–6 mL·kg^−1^·min^−1^ on average [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA; @Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT] | Moderate (strength, VO₂max); low (individual muscle gain) |
| End of Phase 2 (≈7 months) | Continued gains, slowing; barbell lifts learned | Trained muscles typically 5–10% larger than at the start, wide range [@Ahtiainen2016_heterogeneity; @Hubal2005_variability] | Leaner if the deficit was kept; waist the main marker | Able to run about 24 min continuously (planned progression) | Low to moderate |
| End of Phase 3 (≈1 year) | Large relative gains; progress per month now clearly slower | Plausibly 2–5 kg lean mass over the year with good adherence (inference, not a measured average) | Lean, maintainable body-fat range | Higher VO₂max; HIIT and run fitness | Low (inference) |
| Years 2+ | Small, steady gains | Each year adds less than the one before; the approximate drug-free upper limit seen in one small study (normalised FFMI ≈ 25) is many years and ~18–24 kg of fat-free mass away [@Kouri1995_FFMI] | Maintenance | Maintained or improved | Low |

The goal is an athletic, lean look rather than maximal size. Because muscle accrues slowly, "too bulky" is not a near-term risk, and you control it directly: once a muscle looks the way you want, its weekly sets drop to a maintenance dose (see [[rule:size-control]]).
principles:
- **Progressive overload, measured.** Add reps, then load, within each exercise's rep range ([[rule:double-progression]]).
- **Hard but not reckless.** Most sets end 1–3 reps short of failure; free-weight compound lifts never go to failure, because you train alone (safety convention). Getting close to failure matters for growth; reaching it adds little [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression; @Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy].
- **Volume where it matters for your look.** Shoulders (especially the lateral deltoid), upper chest, back width and arms get the most weekly sets; legs get enough for athletic proportions, running and hiking [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency].
- **Full range of motion.** It builds muscle at least as well as partial ranges [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta] and improves flexibility about as much as stretching; muscle gained this way does not make you stiff [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROMmeta; @Afonso2021_STvsStretchMeta].
- **Aerobic work that supports, not competes.** At these doses, aerobic training does not measurably blunt muscle or strength gains in untrained people [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA; @Petre2021_trainingStatusMA], and it is scheduled on separate days.
- **Variety with anchors.** A few anchor lifts stay fixed within a block so progress is visible; accessories rotate between blocks to keep training interesting [@Kassiano2022_variationSR; @BazValle2019_variationMotivation].
- **Decisions from trends.** Weight (7-day average), waist (weekly), logged performance and tape measures drive adjustments; single readings never do.

items.dose: 6 reps, 2–3 s pause at the bottom

wu-full-a.rationale:
**Why a two-layer warm-up.** A general layer (easy cardio) raises muscle temperature; a specific layer (dynamic drills, then lighter ramp-up sets of your first exercises) rehearses the movements you are about to load. Warm-ups improved short-term performance in most outcomes studied [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance], loaded movement-specific warm-ups improved upper-body strength and power [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup], and adding a general warm-up before a specific one increased leg-press strength in a small crossover trial [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup].

**Why it is a little longer for you.** You train about an hour after waking, which is biologically early in your day. Body temperature is the factor most often linked to time-of-day performance differences, and warm-ups (an extended one judged most effective) reduced the early-day deficit across studies [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation], although in one small lifting study an extended morning warm-up did not fully close it [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts]. Applying this to a late sleeper is an inference.

**Why dynamic, not long static, stretches here.** Holding static stretches of 60 s or more per muscle just before lifting reduces strength and power by about 4–5%; dynamic stretching slightly improves it [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. Long static stretching is saved for the cool-down.

**Why balance practice.** Balance gains are specific to the task practised [@Kummel2016_specificity], and your eyes-open single-leg stance (especially on the left) is well below the average for men your age [@Springer2007_UPST]; a minute of practice every session builds that specific skill.

**Mechanisms.** Higher muscle temperature speeds enzyme kinetics and nerve conduction and lowers tissue viscosity; ramp-up sets add task-specific neural rehearsal. These are physiological explanations; the outcome evidence above is what justifies the routine.

wu-full-b.rationale: Same logic as the A warm-up: a general layer to raise muscle temperature (longer because you train soon after waking), dynamic drills for the joints used today (shoulder blades and upper back for pressing and pulling; ankles and hips for the leg press and split squat), balance practice, then ramp-up sets on the first lifts [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance; @Abad2011_general_specific_warmup; @Behm2016_acute_stretching; @Kummel2016_specificity].

2 × 30 s per leg, left first; progress to eyes closed

wu-upper.rationale: General warm-up, then shoulder-girdle and thoracic drills that prepare the joints you will load, then ramp-up sets on the first press and pull. Balance practice stays in every warm-up because the skill is task-specific and improves with frequent practice [@Kummel2016_specificity; @Lesinski2015_balanceDR]. See the full-body warm-up for the evidence on warm-up structure [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance; @McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup].

items.dose: 6 min (bike or incline walk): easy to moderate
6 reps, 2–3 s pause at the bottom
2 × 30 s per leg, left first; progress to eyes closed

wu-lower.rationale: Lower-body sessions begin with the heaviest, most technical lifts (squat or Romanian deadlift), so the warm-up raises temperature, takes the hips and ankles through the range you will load, and finishes with three ramp-up sets. Dynamic rather than static stretching is used before lifting [@Behm2016_acute_stretching; @Abad2011_general_specific_warmup; @Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT].

items.dose: 6 min (bike or incline walk): easy to moderate
6 reps, 2–3 s pause at the bottom
2 rounds × 3 reaches per leg, left first

wu-lower-athletic.rationale: In Phase 3 the lower-body warm-up also carries the athletic work. Plyometric training reliably improves jumping and reactive strength and also improves balance about as much as balance training does; modest volumes (well under 250 contacts per week) are sufficient [@Markovic2007_vertjump; @RamirezCampillo2023_RSI; @Moran2023_stiffness; @Ramachandran2021_plyobalance]. Change-of-direction and coordination gains are task-specific [@NygaardFalch2019_COD], so ladder and bounding drills are brief primers; the bigger coordination payoff is from a skill you enjoy (dance or a martial art). Doing jumps when fresh, before heavy lifting, keeps landing quality high (practical inference).

items.dose: 4 min easy on the machine you will use

wu-cardio.rationale: A short progressive start lets heart rate, breathing and muscle blood flow rise gradually before steady work. Dynamic leg drills prepare the hips and ankles. Static stretching is kept for afterwards [@Behm2016_acute_stretching; @Fradkin2010_warmup_performance].

items.dose: 8 min: 4 min easy, then 4 min moderate (RPE 5)
2 × 20 s at interval effort, 40 s easy between

wu-intervals.rationale: Hard intervals need a thorough, progressive warm-up: easy then moderate work raises temperature and speeds oxygen-uptake kinetics, and two short pick-ups rehearse the target intensity so the first interval is not a shock. This follows consensus warm-up structure [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi] and the general warm-up evidence [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance].

items.dose: 10 reps, 2 s squeeze at the top
A-skip and high knees, 2 × 15 m each

wu-run.rationale: Brisk walking eases you into running; ankle and hip drills prepare the tissues that take most of running's load; short drills rehearse a tall, quick stride. Warm-ups help performance [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance], but warming up as such has not been shown to prevent running injuries [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi]. The glute bridge and side plank are a brief stand-in for the one pre-run routine with trial support: in adult novice runners, a physiotherapist-supervised hip-and-core programme done before runs lowered injury incidence compared with static stretching (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.45–0.97), whereas an ankle-and-foot programme did not help [@Leppanen2024_RunRCT]. Your short, unsupervised version is an approximation of that programme, not the tested intervention (inference).

wu-test.rationale: Tests are only comparable if the warm-up is identical every time, because temperature and warm-up length change both performance and flexibility measurements [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation; @Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility]. Keep this routine, the time of day and the order of tests the same at every assessment.

items.dose: 2 × 30 s per leg at a strong but tolerable stretch (about 7/10)

cd-full-a.rationale:
**What the cool-down is for, honestly.** An active cool-down does not meaningfully speed recovery, prevent soreness or prevent injury [@VanHooren2018_cooldown], and stretching does not reduce muscle soreness or speed strength recovery to a worthwhile degree [@Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS; @Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery]. The two minutes of easy movement are for comfort as heart rate and breathing settle.

**Why stretch here, then.** Regular static stretching reliably increases range of motion (about 1 standard deviation versus control across 77 studies) [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], and after training is the point where long static holds cannot blunt your lifting. Your toe-touch limitation makes the hamstrings the priority: they are stretched in every session, giving roughly 5 minutes per leg per week, the weekly dose associated with gains [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]. In one small calf-stretching trial, a strong stretch (6–7/10) produced larger gains than a gentle one [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS], although intensity did not clearly change the effect across studies [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. Hip flexors are included because you sit at a desk for nine hours.

**Mechanism.** In programmes of a few weeks, range improves mainly through greater tolerance of the stretch sensation (a nervous-system change) [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance; @Freitas2018_chronic_stretch_mechanics]; more intense or higher-volume programmes can also reduce muscle stiffness and slightly lengthen fascicles [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS; @Panidi2023_stretch_architecture_meta].

items.dose: 2 × 30 s per leg (one straight-knee, one bent-knee)

cd-full-b.rationale: Same purpose as cool-down A: comfort, plus accumulating weekly stretching for range of motion rather than recovery [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM; @VanHooren2018_cooldown]. Hamstrings again (every session), calves (squat depth, running) and chest (pressing posture). Loaded full-range lifting also improves flexibility about as much as stretching does [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM], so the stretching tops up what the training already provides.

cd-upper.rationale: Chest and lat stretches after pressing and pulling; the hamstring stretch keeps your weekly hamstring dose on every training day [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM; @Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. The cool-down is for comfort and range of motion, not for recovery [@VanHooren2018_cooldown].

cd-lower.rationale: After squats, hinges and lunges: hamstrings (your priority), hip flexors (desk job), quadriceps and glutes. Static stretching is done after, not before, heavy leg work [@Behm2016_acute_stretching; @Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM].

items.dose: 2 × 30 s per leg (straight and bent knee)

cd-cardio.rationale: Easy movement lets breathing and heart rate settle; the stretches target the muscles most used in walking, running and cycling and keep your hamstring dose going on non-lifting days [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]. As elsewhere, the purpose is range of motion, not faster recovery [@VanHooren2018_cooldown].

items.dose: 4 min: marching on the spot or stair walking, easy (RPE 2–3) to moderate (RPE 4–5); easy jogging on the spot or skipping only from Phase 2
6 reps, 2–3 s pause at the bottom
10 reps (hands on a table or the floor)

wu-away.rationale:
**The same two layers as the gym warm-up, without a machine.** Easy-to-moderate general movement raises muscle temperature; dynamic drills then take the spine, hips and shoulder blades through the ranges you are about to load, and the first exercise starts with an easier set. Warm-ups improved short-term performance in most outcomes studied [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance], and adding a general warm-up before a specific one increased leg-press strength in a small crossover trial [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup]. You train about an hour after waking, and warm-ups reduced time-of-day performance differences across studies [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]; on a cold day, take 6 min rather than 4 (practical convention).

**Why these drills.** Scapular push-ups and glute bridges rehearse today's push-ups, rows, split squats and hinges at low load (practical convention). Dynamic rather than long static stretching comes before training: static holds of 60 s or more per muscle reduced immediate performance by about 4.6% on average, whereas dynamic stretching slightly improved it [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. Balance practice stays because its gains are specific to the task practised [@Kummel2016_specificity], and your left-leg stance is the weaker one.

items.dose: 2 × 30 s per leg with a towel or belt, about 7/10
2 × 30 s per side (knee on a folded towel)

cd-away.rationale: Same purpose as the gym cool-downs: two minutes of easy walking for comfort while breathing settles, then static stretching for range of motion. Neither the cool-down nor the stretching meaningfully speeds recovery or prevents soreness [@VanHooren2018_cooldown; @Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery], but regular static stretching reliably increases range of motion [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. Your hamstrings are stretched in every session, as in the gym, which with the cardio-day cool-downs gives about 5 minutes per leg per week, the weekly dose associated with gains [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]; the hip-flexor stretch offsets desk sitting and the doorway chest stretch follows the push-ups (practical convention). Stretching probably matters slightly more away from the gym (inference): across 55 studies, resistance training in general improved range of motion about as much as stretching, but the subgroup that trained with body mass only showed no significant gain [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM].

items.dose: 5 min easy walking, building to brisk

wu-away-cardio.rationale: A short progressive start lets heart rate, breathing and muscle blood flow rise gradually before steady walking, stairs or running; leg swings and ankle rocks prepare the hips and ankles. Static stretching is kept for afterwards [@Behm2016_acute_stretching; @Fradkin2010_warmup_performance].

items.dose: 8 min: 4 min easy, then 4 min moderate (RPE 5)
2 × 20 s at interval effort, 40 s easy between

wu-away-intervals.rationale: Hard efforts need a thorough, progressive warm-up: easy then moderate movement raises muscle temperature, and two short pick-ups at interval effort (a brisk 20-s climb, an uphill burst, or 20 s of fast high knees before the circuit) rehearse the target intensity so the first effort is not a shock. This follows consensus warm-up structure [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi] and the general warm-up evidence [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance].

items.dose: 2 × 30 s per leg (straight and bent knee)
2 × 30 s per leg with a towel, about 7/10

cd-away-cardio.rationale: Two minutes of easy walking let breathing and heart rate settle; the stretches target the calves, hamstrings and quadriceps that stairs, hills and brisk walking use most, and keep your hamstring dose going on non-strength days [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]. As elsewhere, the purpose is range of motion, not faster recovery [@VanHooren2018_cooldown].

phases.name: Phase 0 · Orientation
phases.tagline: Learn the gym, measure your starting point, and calibrate your nutrition before changing anything.
phases.purpose:
Three jobs in one week. (1) **Learn**: practise the main movement patterns with deliberately light loads so technique is learned before effort rises. (2) **Measure**: record a standardised baseline (body measurements and photos, resting heart rate, an aerobic walking test, push-ups, pull-ups, a jump, balance and flexibility tests) so every later decision rests on your own data. (3) **Calibrate**: keep eating as you normally do while weighing yourself daily and logging food, because your weight has been stable for six months, which means your current intake roughly equals your current expenditure; that observed number is more accurate than any equation.

Very light first sessions should also limit the severe soreness that unaccustomed training causes (inference), and a first exposure protects against soreness from later bouts: after one damaging bout of an arm exercise, a repeat bout 6 months later caused less soreness (the repeated-bout effect) [@Nosaka2001_RBE_duration; @Hyldahl2017_repeated_bout_effect].
phases.structure:
- **Mon** Technique session A · **Tue** Baseline test session · **Thu** Technique session B · **Sat** Easy aerobic session (learn the talk test).
- Every day: weigh in under the standard protocol; log everything you eat and drink; walk as usual.
- One morning this week: tape measurements and photos ([[ex:test-girths]]) and resting heart rate on three mornings ([[ex:test-rhr]]).
- Effort: stop every set with about **4 reps in reserve**. This week is about learning positions and machine settings, not about effort.

phases.name: Phase 1 · Foundations
phases.tagline: Three full-body sessions and two aerobic sessions a week: technique, first muscle and strength, slow fat loss.
phases.purpose: Build technique and the habit, gain your first muscle and strength, and lose fat slowly at the same time (recomposition). Untrained people respond to modest volumes, so weekly sets start low and rise in steps [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency; @Schoenfeld2017_volume_meta]. Full-body sessions three times a week train every muscle 2–3 times per week, which gives frequent practice of each movement; with volume equal, frequency itself makes little difference to growth [@Schoenfeld2019_frequency_hypertrophy; @RamosCampo2024_split_vs_fullbody], so the choice is about practice and fitting volume into 60-minute sessions.
phases.structure:
- **Strength:** three full-body sessions (A and B alternate: A-B-A one week, B-A-B the next) on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, about 60–65 minutes each including warm-up and cool-down.
- **Aerobic:** Tuesday steady session (20 → 35 min); Saturday steady session in weeks 1–6, then introductory intervals in weeks 7–11. Any steady session can be swapped for a brisk hike, dance class or martial-arts class of similar effort and duration.
- **Rest:** Thursday and Sunday (walk; aim for your step target).
- **Exercise order:** the first exercise of each session is the one you most want to improve; accessories are paired in supersets of non-competing muscles to save time without reducing volume [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].
- **Weekly sets per muscle:** about 4–6 in weeks 1–2, 8–12 in weeks 3–11, counting a set fully for the main muscle and half for synergists [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency].
entry: Phase 0 completed: baseline recorded, technique sessions done.
Maintenance calorie estimate available (from logging plus weigh-ins, or the energy tool).
phases.progression: Use [[rule:double-progression|double progression]] on every exercise: stay at a load until every working set reaches the top of the rep range at the target effort, then add the smallest increment. Effort targets tighten over the phase: **weeks 1–2** about 3–4 reps in reserve (RIR); **weeks 3–6** 2–3 RIR on free weights, about 2 on machines; **weeks 7–11** 2–3 RIR on free weights, 1–2 on machines, 0–2 on isolation exercises (last set may reach failure on machines and cables only). Free-weight compound lifts never go to failure because you train alone (safety convention); stopping short of failure costs little or no strength [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression]. In weeks 5 and 9, take the last set of one machine exercise to failure to check your RIR estimates, which are typically off by about one rep [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy] ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
advance: At least 80% of planned sessions completed over the phase (the app counts your 'done' ticks).
Technique self-check passed on the goblet squat, dumbbell presses and Romanian deadlift (filmed from the side; see each exercise's error list).
Loads or reps improved on most exercises since week 3.
No unresolved pain that changes how you move.
repeat: Most lifts stalled for 3+ weeks despite good sleep and nutrition: repeat weeks 7–12 after reviewing the stall rule.
You feel technique on the dumbbell and hinge patterns is not yet consistent.
regress: A break of more than 3 weeks: go back 2–3 weeks (restart at week 3 if the break exceeded 8 weeks) with loads reduced per [[rule:breaks]].
An injury or illness that stopped training for more than 3 weeks: return to week 3 once cleared; shorter interruptions follow [[rule:breaks]] and [[rule:illness]].

phases.nutrition: Weeks 1–2: keep eating as in Phase 0 and keep logging and weighing daily, which completes the calibration of your maintenance intake (set the check-in tool's goal to 'Calibrate'). From week 3: recomposition, a small energy deficit with high protein, aiming for slow weight loss while strength rises. Targets, the weight-trend band and the adjustment rule are in the [[plan:nutrition|nutrition plan]] and the [[tool:checkin|check-in tool]].
phases.conditioning: Two aerobic sessions per week plus daily steps. Steady sessions build from 20 to 35 minutes at a conversational effort; from week 7 the Saturday session becomes short intervals (1 minute hard, 2 minutes easy), a first exposure to high intensity. Balance practice is in every warm-up; hamstring stretching in every cool-down.

weekPlans.title: Learn the movements
weekPlans.notes: Two sets per exercise, stopping 3–4 reps short of failure. Settle on loads: if a set felt like more than 5 reps in reserve, go heavier next time. Expect some soreness after the first sessions; it fades quickly. Nutrition: no change yet; keep logging food and weighing daily to finish calibrating your maintenance intake.

weekPlans.notes: Three sets on the main lifts; split squats, calf raises and arm work start. Add load whenever every set reaches the top of its rep range at the target effort. Waist every week; all girths and photos at the end of week 4.

weekPlans.title: Build the base
weekPlans.notes: Week 5: calibrate your effort estimates once (last set of the leg press or chest press to momentary failure, see the RIR calibration rule). Waist every week.

weekPlans.notes: Isolation exercises go to 3 sets; machines may be taken to 1 rep in reserve and isolation exercises to failure on the last set (machines and cables only). Saturday becomes intervals. Waist every week; all girths and photos at week 8. Week 9: repeat the RIR calibration.
