phases.name: Phase 2 · Development
phases.tagline: Upper/lower split four days a week, barbell lifts, 4 × 4 intervals and a run–walk base.
phases.purpose: Raise weekly volume for the muscles that shape an athletic upper body (lateral and rear deltoids, upper chest, back width, arms) to about 12–16 sets, keep legs at roughly 10–13 for proportion and running, learn the barbell squat and Romanian deadlift in a rack with safety arms, and build aerobic fitness with intervals that meet the criteria linked to the largest VO₂max gains (intervals of ≥2 minutes, ≥15 minutes of hard work, sustained over weeks) [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA; @Helgerud2007_4x4RCT; @Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Running starts as run–walk, and each run stays within about 10% of your longest run in the previous 30 days.
phases.structure:
- **Mon** Upper A (heavier pressing) · **Tue** Lower A (squat) · **Wed** 4 × 4 intervals · **Thu** Upper B (pull-up and pulling emphasis) · **Fri** Lower B (hinge and single-leg) · **Sat** run–walk (or a hike, ride or dance class of similar length) · **Sun** rest.
- Each muscle is trained twice a week; each upper session starts with a different priority lift, and some accessories sit on lower days (a third lateral-raise exposure) [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta].
- Mild daily undulation: the first lift on 'A' days uses lower reps (heavier), 'B' days moderate reps.
- Aerobic work is on separate days from lifting, which avoids the small same-session interference seen for explosive strength [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA].
- Interval sessions use the bike, rower or incline treadmill walking (not running) until you can run 20 minutes continuously.
entry: Phase 1 advance criteria met (or Phase 1 repeated).
You can perform the goblet squat and dumbbell Romanian deadlift with consistent technique at 2 reps in reserve.
phases.progression: Double progression continues. On the main barbell lifts, keep 2–3 reps in reserve and never grind a rep without safety arms in place. Weeks 1–3 introduce the barbell at moderate reps (8–10); from week 9 the first lift on A days moves to 5–8 reps. The planned lighter week (week 8) halves sets; take extra lighter weeks only when the [[rule:deload]] triggers. If a priority muscle's girth has not changed after 12 weeks of good adherence, add 2–4 sets per week for it ([[rule:lagging-muscle]]).
advance: At least 80% of planned sessions completed.
Barbell squat and Romanian deadlift performed with consistent technique (filmed check) at the prescribed effort.
Continuous running of about 20+ minutes reached (or a deliberate choice to keep aerobic work on other machines).
repeat: Adherence below 80% or a long disruption: repeat weeks 9–16.
Running progression stalled or interrupted by niggles: repeat the run–walk weeks you missed before progressing.
regress: Recurrent pain with barbell lifts: return to the Phase 1 dumbbell/machine versions for those patterns for 4 weeks and reassess technique.
A break of more than 3 weeks: go back 2–3 weeks with reduced loads per [[rule:breaks]]; after more than 8 weeks, restart Phase 1 at week 3.

expected.value: Continued slow gain; the clearest changes in shoulder, chest and arm girths
expected.note: Gains slowed after the first 6 weeks of continuous training in one small trial [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous]; individual responses vary widely [@Hubal2005_variability].

expected.value: Further rise; 4 × 4 intervals add a little more than continuous training alone
expected.note: HIIT vs continuous ≈ +1.4 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ on average, low certainty [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT].

expected.value: About 24 min continuous by week 15
expected.note: Planned progression; injuries are common in novice runners whatever the plan [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence].

expected.value: Sets of 6–8 bodyweight reps for many people by the end

phases.nutrition: At the start of this phase the [[rule:phase-nutrition]] decides between continuing the recomposition deficit and switching to maintenance or a small surplus, based on your waist and body-fat trend at the end of Phase 1.
phases.conditioning: Wednesday: 4 × 4-minute intervals at a hard effort (RPE 8–9) with 3-minute easy recoveries (3-minute intervals in weeks 1–3). Saturday: run–walk, each run within ~10% of your longest run in the previous 30 days ([[rule:running]]); swap for a hike or dance class when you prefer, but repeat a run–walk step you skipped rather than jumping ahead. Daily steps continue.

weekPlans.title: Transition to upper/lower
weekPlans.notes: New split, new barbell lifts: keep reps moderate and effort conservative while you learn the squat and Romanian deadlift in the rack. Set the safety arms every time. Week 2: RIR calibration on a machine exercise.

weekPlans.title: Accumulate
weekPlans.notes: Full volume. Waist every week; girths and photos at week 4. Week 7: RIR calibration on a machine exercise.

weekPlans.title: Lighter week
weekPlans.notes: Half the sets, more reps in reserve, same exercises and loads (or ~10% lighter). Use the week to swap any accessory you are bored with for a listed alternative. All girths and photos.

weekPlans.title: Build
weekPlans.notes: The first lift on A days moves to 5–8 reps (heavier). Priority muscles get a 4th set. Waist every week; girths and photos at week 12. Week 12: RIR calibration.

params.rwText: 24:00 continuous easy running (if that feels like too big a step from 11-minute bouts, run 2 × 12:00 with a 1:00 walk this week and go continuous next week)

weekPlans.title: Reassess
tests: Test session (Wednesday): 2.4 km run test if you can run 20+ min continuously (otherwise the walking test), push-ups, pull-ups, broad jump, balance and flexibility
weekPlans.notes: Lighter lifting so the tests reflect fitness, not fatigue.

phases.name: Phase 3 · Athletic
phases.tagline: Three 8-week blocks: hypertrophy, strength and power, then physique and conditioning, with jumps and agility built into warm-ups.
phases.purpose: Keep building muscle while adding the athletic qualities on your list: maximal strength, power, agility and conditioning. Rotating emphasis in blocks provides planned variety (your stated risk is boredom) without random exercise-hopping, which can slow progress [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. Periodisation model matters little for hypertrophy; a heavier block mainly helps maximal strength [@Moesgaard2022_periodization; @Currier2026_ACSMpositionStand].
phases.structure:
- Same weekly frame as Phase 2: Upper A, Lower A, intervals, Upper B, Lower B, long session, rest.
- **Block 1 (weeks 1–8) Hypertrophy:** main lifts 6–10 reps; new exercise variants (Smith-machine incline press, chin-ups, cable curls, reverse lunges).
- **Block 2 (weeks 9–16) Strength and power:** main lifts 4–6 reps at 2–3 reps in reserve (barbell bench press and trap-bar deadlift enter, always with safety arms or a trap bar); jump training in lower-body warm-ups (≈36 contacts per session).
- **Block 3 (weeks 17–24) Physique and conditioning:** main lifts 6–10 reps; an extra set for your chosen priority muscles; agility and bounding drills in lower warm-ups; intervals plus a tempo or long session.
- Weeks 8 and 16 are lighter; week 24 is a full reassessment.
entry: Comfortable with the barbell squat, Romanian deadlift and pull-ups (assisted or bodyweight) at the prescribed effort.
phases.progression: Double progression within each block. At each block change, start the new rep range about 2 reps in reserve below your estimated limit (use the [[tool:e1rm|e1RM tool]] from your logged sets). In Block 2, heavy sets stay at 2–3 reps in reserve: you train alone, and strength gains are similar without failure [@Grgic2022_failure_meta; @Wu2026_nonfailure_meta].
advance: At least 80% of planned sessions completed.
Reassessment done (week 24) and goals reviewed with the [[tool:transition|transition checklist]].
repeat: If a block was badly disrupted, repeat that block before moving on.
regress: Recurrent joint pain with heavy (4–6 rep) work: return to Block 1 rep ranges for those lifts.
A break of more than 3 weeks: go back 2–3 weeks with reduced loads per [[rule:breaks]]; after more than 8 weeks, restart Phase 1 at week 3.

expected.value: Clearer gains in Block 2 on the trained lifts (strength is specific to load and exercise)
expected.note: [@Lopez2021_load_NMA; @Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]

expected.value: Improved jump distance/height and drill times; mostly specific to what is practised
expected.note: [@Markovic2007_vertjump; @NygaardFalch2019_COD]

expected.value: Slower than year one; small yearly gains become the norm
expected.note: Inference from the slowing seen within single trials and the approximate natural upper limit [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous; @Kouri1995_FFMI].

phases.nutrition: If you met the leanness criterion, a small energy surplus supports muscle gain with limited fat gain; otherwise stay at maintenance or a small deficit. The [[rule:phase-nutrition]] decides.
phases.conditioning: Intervals weekly (4 × 4 in Blocks 1 and 3; 6 × 2 minutes very hard in Block 2), plus a long session (continuous run, hike, ride or a dance or martial-arts class). Jumps and agility live in the lower-body warm-ups.

weekPlans.title: Block 1 · Hypertrophy
weekPlans.notes: New variants for the main lifts; rebuild loads over the first two weeks. Long run 40–45 minutes easy (or a hike, ride or class).

weekPlans.title: Lighter week
weekPlans.notes: Half the sets. Girths and photos. Choose the exercises for Block 2 from the listed options.

weekPlans.title: Block 2 · Strength and power
weekPlans.notes: Heavier main lifts (4–6 reps) with safety arms set every time; jumps in lower warm-ups. Do not take heavy barbell sets to failure.

weekPlans.title: Lighter week and mid-point tests
tests: Push-ups, pull-ups, broad jump (end of the Upper B and Lower B sessions)

weekPlans.title: Block 3 · Physique and conditioning
weekPlans.notes: Pick one or two priority muscles (e.g., lateral deltoids and upper back); they get an extra set. Agility and bounding in lower warm-ups.

phases.name: Phase 4 · Continuation
phases.tagline: Repeating 12-week cycles: choose an emphasis, keep progressing or hold the physique you want.
phases.purpose: From the second year the programme becomes self-directed within a fixed frame. Each 12-week cycle you choose an emphasis (a lagging muscle, strength on a lift, running, or a skill such as a martial art), keep everything else at a maintenance dose, and reassess. When you are happy with a muscle's size, move it to maintenance volume (about 6–8 weekly sets) and spend the effort elsewhere ([[rule:size-control]]). Strength and muscle can be maintained with far less training than it took to build them [@Spiering2021_minimalDose; @Bickel2011_maintenanceDose].
phases.structure:
- Same weekly frame as Phases 2–3.
- **Weeks 1–5:** moderate reps (6–10 on main lifts); **week 6** lighter; **weeks 7–11:** heavier main lifts (5–8); **week 12:** reassess and plan the next cycle.
- Swap accessories and the long-session activity every cycle to keep training fresh.
phases.progression: Double progression; autoregulated deloads ([[rule:deload]]); volume per muscle set by your emphasis for the cycle (priority 12–16 sets per week; maintenance 6–8).
advance: At week 12, decide the next cycle's emphasis using your test results, tape measurements and what you enjoy; then start week 1 again.
regress: Busy, travelling or recovering from illness: switch to [[phase:pm|Maintenance mode]] and return when life settles.

expected.value: Small yearly gains; or stable if you choose maintenance
expected.note: [@Kouri1995_FFMI; @Spiering2021_minimalDose]

phases.nutrition: Usually maintenance. Use short, deliberate surplus or deficit periods for specific aims, steered by the weekly check-in.
phases.conditioning: Keep one interval session and one long session each week; that preserves VO₂max well [@Spiering2021_minimalDose].

phases.name: Maintenance mode
phases.switchHint: busy week: two short gym sessions
phases.tagline: Two short full-body sessions and two short aerobic sessions: the minimum that holds your progress during busy weeks.
phases.purpose: When work, travel (with a gym; without one, use [[phase:pa|Away mode]]), illness recovery or motivation dips make the full programme unrealistic, this keeps what you have built. Strength and muscle are retained for weeks to months with roughly one-third of the usual volume if effort stays high, and short intense aerobic sessions maintain VO₂max [@Spiering2021_minimalDose; @Bickel2011_maintenanceDose; @Iversen2021_time_efficient]. Short breaks cost little in any case: 3-week breaks did not reduce long-term gains in one small trial [@Ogasawara2013_periodicVsContinuous], and losses grow with the length of the break [@Bosquet2013_detrainingMeta].
phases.structure:
- Two full-body sessions (about 40 minutes) on any non-consecutive days.
- One short interval session and one steady session (or a hike/class).
- Sets end 1–3 reps short of failure at your usual loads.
entry: Use whenever you need it: tap **Switch** next to Maintenance mode on Today. The app remembers your current week and shows a one-tap return.
phases.progression: None needed: the goal is to hold. Keep loads the same and effort high.
advance: Return to your previous phase and week when normal life resumes, with the Return button on Today (see [[rule:breaks]] if more than 3 weeks have passed).
repeat: Repeat weekly for as long as needed.

expected.value: Largely maintained for weeks to months
expected.note: [@Spiering2021_minimalDose; @Bickel2011_maintenanceDose]

phases.nutrition: Eat at maintenance; keep protein high.
phases.conditioning: One interval session (e.g., 4 × 4 or 6 × 2 minutes) and one steady or long session.

phases.name: Away mode (no equipment)
phases.switchHint: no gym or weights: bodyweight sessions
phases.tagline: Three no-equipment full-body sessions and two aerobic sessions a week for trips and closed gyms: effort replaces load, ladders replace plates.
phases.purpose:
**When to use it.** When you are away from any gym for more than a few days with no machines or weights: a trip, a holiday, a family visit or a closed gym. Any gym beats it, even a basic hotel gym or a day pass, so use one whenever you can, swapping exercises as needed ([[rule:substitution]]), and stay in your phase. Gaps of 1–4 days need nothing: Away mode is optional and there is nothing to make up ([[rule:away]]).

**What it maintains or builds.** With light loads, how close a set ends to [[term:momentary-failure|failure]] matters a great deal: in 25 untrained men, knee-extension sets at 30% of [[term:1rm|1RM]] grew the quadriceps 7.8% over 8 weeks when taken to failure but only 2.8% (not significant) when stopped short [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load], and with sets to failure, light and heavy loads built similar muscle across 21 studies [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta]. Bodyweight exercises ([[term:calisthenics|calisthenics]]) have been tested directly, in small trials: push-ups to failure grew the chest (+18.3%) and triceps (+9.5%) about as much as a bench press at a matched light load in 18 young men with at least a year of lifting experience [@Kikuchi2017_pushupVsBench], and suspension-strap training matched machines for muscle and strength in 42 untrained older adults [@Soligon2020_suspensionVsTraditional]. Keeping muscle takes far less than building it: in young adults, one-third of the original training dose preserved the muscle gained over 16 weeks for a further 32 weeks [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose; @Spiering2021_minimalDose]. Away mode gives about 5–9 hard sets a week for most muscles, with calves and biceps getting less (helper muscles counted at half a set [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency]), so it should hold your muscle in Phases 2–4 and is close to a growth dose in [[phase:p1|Phase 1]] (inference).

**Its limits, honestly.**
- The **lats, biceps and lateral deltoids** are the hardest to load without a bar or band (inference). Table rows, backpack rows and bottle or backpack lateral raises are the best available. A long loop resistance band is the most useful single purchase if trips become common ([[dec:D30]]): elastic bands matched conventional training for strength gains in a small meta-analysis of mixed populations [@Lopes2019_elasticVsConventionalMeta], and an EMG study judged them feasible for rows and pulldowns [@Iversen2017_bandsMultiJointEMG].
- **Heavy-load strength is partly specific.** Light loads built less 1RM strength than heavy ones [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta; @Lopez2021_load_NMA], and dynamic training improved strength in the trained movement about twice as much as untrained isometric strength ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.98 vs 0.42) [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta], so your first gym session back may feel harder than your muscle size would suggest (inference).
- The maintenance trials kept the usual relative load [@Spiering2021_minimalDose]; Away mode swaps load for effort, so applying them here is inference. In the closest comparison, a non-randomised trial in previously inactive adults aged 30–64 whose bodyweight sets were not explicitly taken to failure, a body mass-based programme grew the quadriceps somewhat less than free weights (about +3.6% vs +6.3%; difference p = 0.051, just short of significance) and did not significantly raise knee-extension strength [@Ogawa2023_bodyMassVsFreeWeight].
phases.structure:
- **Strength:** three full-body sessions, A and B alternating (A-B-A one week, B-A-B the next) on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, about 55 minutes each including warm-up and cool-down; each has a ≈25-minute short version.
- **Aerobic:** Tuesday steady session (brisk walking, hills or stairs, or a hike, swim, ride or class) and Saturday intervals (stairs, a hill or a low-impact bodyweight circuit; a second steady session if your gym phase has no intervals yet).
- **Rest:** Thursday and Sunday. Keep walking every day.
- **Ladders replace plates.** Each exercise has a [[term:progression-ladder|progression ladder]]: harder leverage (feet raised, body nearer horizontal), more range, one leg instead of two, a slower lowering, pauses, then a loaded backpack. Weigh the backpack on your scale: your weight holding it minus your weight without it (1 L of water ≈ 1 kg).
- **[[term:superset|Supersets]]** pair exercises that do not compete (push-ups with rows, hinges with pike push-ups), which saves time without reducing gains [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].
- **Weekly sets per muscle:** about 4–6 in week 1 and 5–9 from week 2 for most muscles; calves and biceps get less.
- **What you need:** floor space, a chair, a bed or sofa, a sturdy table or a door frame, stairs or a step, a towel and a backpack. Optional: a long loop resistance band or a bar in a park.
entry: You are away from any gym, or it is closed, for more than a few days; for 1–4 days Away mode is optional ([[rule:away]]).
No illness and no pain that changes how you move; after illness, follow [[rule:illness]] first.
Tap **Switch** next to Away mode on Today: the app remembers your current phase and week and offers a one-tap return.
phases.progression:
**Double progression by rung.** [[rule:double-progression]] applies to the [[term:progression-ladder|ladder]] instead of the plates: stay on a rung until every working set reaches the top of the rep range at the target effort, then move one rung up and restart near the bottom of the range. Reps can rise before load: in an 8-week lower-body trial in trained people, progressing reps at a constant load built muscle and strength about as well as progressing load [@Plotkin2022_loadVsRepProgression]. A slower lowering (3–4 s) is a legitimate rung, because repetition durations of about 0.5–8 s gave similar growth when sets went to failure [@Schoenfeld2015_rep_duration].

**A rep ceiling.** When a rung allows more than about 30 reps at the target effort, move up rather than doing ever-longer sets. Sets of 20–25 reps to failure built muscle like sets of 8–12 in trained men [@Morton2016_20to25repsTrained], and every arm trained with 30–40RM or 8–12RM sets gained about 0.25 cm of muscle thickness [@Bell2023_30to40RMvs8to12RM], but loads of about 15–20% of 1RM gave smaller gains in two trials [@Lasevicius2018_20to80pct1RM; @Buckner2019_veryLowLoadArms] and similar thickness gains but no 1RM gain in a third [@Jessee2018_veryLowLoadLegs]. Effort estimates were also less accurate in sets of more than 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy].

**Effort.** Week 1 of each trip stops 2–3 reps short of failure while you find your rungs. From week 2, most sets end 1–2 reps short and isolation sets 0–1, and the last set of push-ups, rows and split squats may go to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]]: with no bar to get stuck under, that is safe (practical convention). The exceptions are the Nordic curl, where every rep is a maximal effort to slow the fall, so the rep count rather than reps in reserve sets its dose (see its note in session B), and any exercise where balance fails before the muscle does. If you left the gym in Phase 0 or Phase 1 weeks 1–6, keep every set at 2–3 reps in reserve and skip the failure sets for the whole trip: like the gym programme, effort rises only once you have practised judging it (practical convention).
advance: When a gym is available again, tap **Return** on Today to go back to your previous phase and week, and read [[rule:away]] before the first session back.

If you trained at least twice a week while away, start at your previous loads; the first session may feel harder (inference), because strength is partly specific to the trained lift and 1RM strength grows more with heavy loads [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta; @Schoenfeld2017_load_meta]. If your reps fall 2 or more short of the range, use about 90% of the load for the rest of that week (inference).
If you trained less than twice a week while away, treat the trip as a break: [[rule:breaks]], counting the days from your last gym session.
repeat: Repeats for as long as you are away: after week 3 it continues from week 2, so only the first week of each trip is introductory.

Each new trip starts at week 1, because new or long-unpractised exercises bring soreness. If your last trip was only a few weeks ago and the exercises still feel familiar, you may start at week 2 with **Make this my current week** on the week page.
regress: Soreness that still limits movement on the day of the next session: do that session at week-1 effort (2 sets, 2–3 reps in reserve) or use an easier rung for the sore muscle. Soreness after new exercises is expected and fades with repetition (the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]]).

Pain in a joint or tendon, rather than effort or ordinary muscle soreness: follow [[rule:pain]] and use an easier rung or the listed alternative, such as [[ex:sliding-leg-curl]] for Nordic curls or a [[ex:split-squat|split squat]] with the rear foot on the floor for the Bulgarian split squat.

Very dark (tea- or cola-coloured) urine, or muscle pain and swelling far beyond what the session should cause: stop training and get a same-day medical assessment at an emergency department ([[plan:safety]]). Exertional [[term:rhabdomyolysis|rhabdomyolysis]] is uncommon, but unaccustomed exercise is one of its recognised causes [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo].

expected.value: Maintained over a typical trip; in Phase 1, possibly still growing slowly
expected.note: One-third of the usual dose preserved muscle gains in young adults [@Bickel2011_maintenanceDose], and light loads taken to failure built muscle like heavy ones [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta]; that bodyweight training does the same is partly inference: in the closest trial it grew the quadriceps, though somewhat less than free weights [@Ogawa2023_bodyMassVsFreeWeight]. Even complete breaks of 2–3 weeks did not significantly reduce muscle size in two small trials [@Ogasawara2011_threeWeekBreakBench; @Hwang2017_twoWeekDetraining], although another measured a 6% fall in thigh-muscle area after 2 weeks off, part of which may have been lost swelling [@McMahon2019_twoFourWeekDetraining].

expected.metric: Gym strength (loads on your usual lifts)
expected.value: Largely kept; the first sessions back may feel harder than expected
expected.note: Light-load training builds less 1RM strength than heavy-load training [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta], and strength gains are partly specific to the trained movement [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]. Complete breaks of 2–3 weeks did not significantly reduce bench-press 1RM or leg-press strength in small trials [@Ogasawara2011_threeWeekBreakBench; @Hwang2017_twoWeekDetraining].

expected.value: Likely to improve: more reps or a higher rung
expected.note: Strength gains are largest in the trained movement [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]; progressive push-up training raised push-up level more than bench pressing did over 4 weeks in 23 moderately trained men [@Kotarsky2018_progressivePushup].

expected.value: Maintained if the interval session stays hard
expected.note: Endurance performance was maintained for up to 15 weeks of reduced training when intensity was kept [@Spiering2021_minimalDose]; in one small trial, stair climbing raised VO₂max in sedentary young women [@Boreham2005_stairClimbing].

expected.value: Marked after the first sessions of new exercises (especially Nordic curls and split squats); much less from week 2
expected.note: In 13 trained men, a first session of 24 Nordic curls raised soreness on days 2–3 and kept eccentric strength down for up to 3 days; the same session 4 weeks later caused smaller, shorter changes [@Coratella2025_NHEmuscleDamageRBE]. In untrained people, one earlier bout cut later soreness most when it came 2–4 days before [@Boyd2023_preconditioningEIMDmeta], so week 1 should already protect week 2 (inference).

expected.value: Stable at maintenance intake with daily walking; travel food and salt can shift scale weight through water
expected.note: Cutting daily steps by about 80–90% for two weeks lowered insulin sensitivity and leg lean mass in small studies [@KroghMadsen2010_twoWeekStepReduction; @BowdenDavies2018_stepReductionMetabolic]: keep walking.

phases.nutrition: Eat at maintenance: set the [[tool:checkin|check-in tool]]'s goal to 'Maintenance' for the trip, and back to your phase's goal when you return. A trip is not the time to push a deficit: lean-mass gains were smaller during an energy deficit in trials [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass], and your loads are lighter than usual. Keep protein at or above your floor of 125 g a day (1.6 g/kg) as a 7-day average, aiming for your usual 140–155 g; in a between-trial analysis the fat-free-mass benefit of extra protein flattened at about 1.6 g/kg/day [@Morton2018_proteinRT]. The practical rule is protein at every meal: eggs, curd, milk, paneer, chicken, fish or mutton dishes, and dal with rice or roti are easy to find almost anywhere in India (practical convention). See the [[plan:nutrition|nutrition plan]] for eating while away. Pause daily weigh-ins until you are back on your own scale, because another scale may read differently; your trend resumes when you return (practical convention).
phases.conditioning:
Two aerobic sessions a week, as in the gym phases. **Tuesday, steady:** 30–35 min of brisk walking at a conversational effort, on hills or stairs if you have them, or a hike, swim, ride or class of similar length. **Saturday, intervals:** 4–6 × 2 min hard / 2 min easy on stairs, a hill or, only if your phase already includes running, a run ([[ex:cardio-noeq-intervals]]). If your gym phase has no interval session yet (Phase 0, or Phase 1 before week 7), make Saturday a second steady session instead, and in the rest of Phase 1 keep the hard efforts at RPE 7–8, as in your gym intervals (practical convention). A low-impact bodyweight circuit is the fallback, because bodyweight-only intervals improved cardiorespiratory fitness less than running or cycling training in pooled trials [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta].

**Every day:** keep walking. A trip can easily cut your daily steps, and in small studies cutting steps by about 80–90% for two weeks lowered insulin sensitivity, fitness and leg lean mass [@KroghMadsen2010_twoWeekStepReduction; @BowdenDavies2018_stepReductionMetabolic], and one week of it lowered muscle protein synthesis by about 27% (a mechanistic measure) [@Shad2019_stepReductionMPS]. On a day with no time for a session, three vigorous climbs of a 3-flight (60-step) stairwell spread across the day still count: done on 3 days a week for 6 weeks, that raised VO₂peak modestly compared with controls in a small trial in sedentary young adults [@Jenkins2019_stairSnacks]. Balance practice stays in every strength warm-up and hamstring stretching in every cool-down.

weekPlans.title: First week away: find your levels
weekPlans.notes: Two sets of everything, stopping 2–3 reps short of failure, while you find the right rung for each exercise: if a set ends with more than about 4 reps in reserve, or passes the top of its range easily, use the next rung next time. **Nordic curls: 2 sets of 3–5 only**, however easy they feel. Expect soreness after exercises you have not done before: the protection that training gives against soreness seems to be partly specific to the exercise (inference), so the gym does not fully prepare you for Nordic curls or for split-squat and lunge variants you have not been doing there. Intervals: 4 efforts while you learn the stairs or route; walk down slowly, because stair descents are eccentric work for the thighs and can leave them sore at first (muscle physiology). Keep walking every day and eat protein at every meal.

weekPlans.title: Hold or build
weekPlans.notes: Primary exercises 3 sets, secondary 2, isolation 3, core 2. Most sets end 1–2 reps short of failure and isolation sets 0–1; the last set of push-ups, rows and split squats may go to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]]. If you left the gym in Phase 0 or Phase 1 weeks 1–6, keep every set at 2–3 reps in reserve and skip the failure sets for the whole trip: like the gym programme, effort rises only once you have practised judging it (practical convention). Nordic curls: 3 × 3–8, dosed by reps rather than reps in reserve: end a set at 8, or sooner when your break point comes clearly earlier than on the first rep. Move up a rung whenever every set reaches the top of its range at the target effort; above about 30 reps, move up rather than going longer. Intervals: 6 efforts. After week 3 the app repeats from week 2.

p0-learn-a.name: Technique session A
p0-learn-a.summary: Your first session: learn seven exercises with light loads. Two easy sets each, stopping about 4 reps before you would have to stop. Note machine settings in your logging app.

items.load: A load you could push about 14 times; stop at 10.
Light dumbbells; focus on the shoulder-blade set-up and a deep, controlled lowering.
Light dumbbells. Your range ends where your back would start to round; with tight hamstrings that may be around knee height at first, and that is fine.
Very light (often 2–5 kg).

main.rationale: Light, low-volume first exposures teach positions while limiting the severe soreness of unaccustomed exercise (inference); a first bout also protects against soreness from later bouts, for months after a damaging bout in one study [@Nosaka2001_RBE_duration; @Hyldahl2017_repeated_bout_effect]. Machines and dumbbells are used because they are easy to learn and safe without a spotter (practical convention), and machine training built muscle as well as free-weight training in direct comparisons [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].

p0-learn-a.record: For every set: exercise, load, reps and an effort rating (RPE; this week should feel like RPE 6). Add machine settings (seat height, pin positions) to each exercise's notes.

p0-learn-b.name: Technique session B
p0-learn-b.summary: Learn the squat pattern, incline pressing, the split squat, the seated leg curl, the shoulder press and an anti-rotation core exercise. Two easy sets each.

items.load: A light dumbbell or kettlebell (often 8–14 kg); go as deep as you can with heels down and a neutral back (your screening squat says you can).
Bodyweight; hold a rack or wall for balance. Left leg first.

main.rationale: Completes the first exposure to every movement pattern used in Phase 1: squat, incline press, single-leg work (your left leg balances less well than your right), knee flexion with the hamstrings lengthened, overhead press and anti-rotation bracing [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl; @Chaves2020_inclineVsFlat].

p0-learn-b.record: Load, reps and RPE for each set; machine settings; for the split squat, note whether the left side felt different from the right.

p0-baseline.name: Baseline test session
p0-baseline.summary: Your reference point. Do the tests in this order, with this warm-up, at your usual training time; repeat them identically at every reassessment.

items.dose: 1.6 km walk as fast as you can (treadmill at 1% incline or a flat measured route); record time and immediate 15-s pulse
items.note: Rest 10–15 minutes before the next tests.

items.dose: 1 maximal set, dead hang, no swinging (after 3 min rest)
Eyes open and closed, each leg, best of 3 (max 45 s)

main.rationale: These field tests need no laboratory equipment and are reliable enough to track change when the protocol is standardised [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test; @Powden2015_WBLT_reliability; @Springer2007_UPST]. The walking test estimates VO₂max safely for someone who has not trained; running tests come later. Conditions (time of day, warm-up, food, test order) are kept identical because they can shift results by amounts similar to real change: in one small study, time of day and warm-up length alone shifted whole-body flexibility by 2–3 cm [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility].

p0-baseline.record: Write every result (with the date, time of day and test conditions) into the app's check-in notes or your logging app's notes, and keep it with your baseline photos and girths.

p0-aerobic.name: Easy aerobic: learn your effort zones
p0-aerobic.summary: Twenty minutes of steady, conversational effort. Practise the talk test and match it to the RPE scale.

items.dose: 20 min at RPE 3–4: you can speak in full sentences

main.rationale: Comfortable speech is possible below the first ventilatory threshold and becomes difficult close to it, so the talk test is a practical, equipment-free intensity guide [@Persinger2004_talkTest; @ReedPipe2014_talkTestReview].

p0-aerobic.record: Machine, duration, distance (if shown) and an overall RPE for the session.

p1-a.name: Full body A
p1-a.summary: Squat pattern, incline press + pulldown, hinge + lateral raise, then arms and core. Supersets pair muscles that do not compete, so volume stays high in about an hour.

main.rationale:
**Selection.** The incline press comes first among the presses because upper-chest development was greater with incline than flat pressing in untrained men in one small trial [@Chaves2020_inclineVsFlat]; the overhead triceps extension loads the long head in a stretched position and grew the triceps about 1.4–1.5 times more than pushdowns [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]; lateral raises grew the lateral deltoid similarly with dumbbells or cables [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable], and that muscle is the main driver of shoulder width (anatomical inference). The Romanian deadlift trains the hamstrings at long lengths, and full-range training is your main flexibility tool [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROMmeta].

**Dose.** Rep ranges of 8–12 for compound lifts and 10–20 for isolation are all within the range that builds muscle equally when sets are hard [@Lopez2021_load_NMA]; rest of 1.5–2 minutes on compounds is enough, since growth benefited slightly from resting more than 60 s but not appreciably beyond about 90 s [@Singer2024_rest_meta]; supersets of non-competing muscles cut session time without reducing gains [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].

**Effort.** Free-weight lifts stay 2–3 reps short of failure because growth is similar to, or only slightly less than, training to failure, recovery is faster, and you have no spotter [@Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression; @Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy; @MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery].

p1-a.shortVersion: Short on time (≈35 min)? Do the warm-up, then 2 sets each of the goblet squat, the incline press + pulldown superset and the RDL + lateral raise superset; skip arms and core; finish with the hamstring stretch only.
p1-a.record: Load, reps and RPE (or RIR) for every working set; ramp-up sets need not be logged. Note anything that felt wrong technically and any pain (location, 0–10).

p1-b.name: Full body B
p1-b.summary: Pull-up practice, leg press, flat press + row, split squat, then leg curl + lateral raise and calf raise + Pallof press.

items.load: Bodyweight. Practice sets that stop well short of failure; if one clean rep is not yet possible, use the assisted machine or slow 3–5 s negatives. In weeks 1–2, use enough assistance that each set leaves about 3 reps in reserve (with a 3-rep maximum, even an unassisted single leaves only 2).
items.note: From week 3, alternate with the calf raise: pull-up set, calf-raise set, then rest. Add a rep to each set when all sets feel easy; at 3 × 5, move to the progression on the exercise page.
Done in the rest between pull-up sets (calves and lats do not compete).

items.warmupSets: 2–3 ramp sets (~50% × 8, ~70% × 4, plus ~85% × 2 once the working load is 60 kg or more)

items.note: Left leg first; match the reps on the right. Then go straight to the Pallof press.

main.rationale:
**Selection.** Pull-up practice comes first while you are fresh because it is a specific skill goal (strength gains are greatest for what is trained first and most specifically) [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta]. The leg press lets you push close to failure safely alone; seated leg curls grew the hamstrings more than lying curls because the hip-flexed position lengthens them [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]; standing calf raises grow the gastrocnemius far more than seated ones [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf]. The split squat adds single-leg work for your weaker left side; unilateral and bilateral training built muscle similarly (very imprecise evidence), and each improved its own task most [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta].

**Dose and effort.** As in session A [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency; @Robinson2024_RIR_metaregression].

p1-b.shortVersion: Short on time (≈35 min)? Warm-up; pull-up practice (2 sets); leg press (2 sets); the press + row superset (2 rounds); leg curl + lateral raise superset (2 rounds); hamstring stretch.
p1-b.record: Load, reps and RPE for every working set. For pull-ups, record assistance (kg on the machine) or 'negative' if used. For split squats, log left and right reps.

p1-aero.name: Steady aerobic
p1-aero.summary: Continuous conversational effort on any machine (incline treadmill walk is the default), or a brisk walk outdoors. Duration grows across the phase.

items.dose: {{z2min}} min at RPE 3–4 (talk test: full sentences)

main.rationale: Any structured aerobic training raises VO₂max substantially in untrained adults; moderate continuous training adds about 5 mL·kg^−1^·min^−1^ on average [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA; @Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Starting with conversational effort builds tolerance before intervals. Training 'just below the first threshold' is effective but not uniquely so [@Storoschuk2025_zone2Review]. On separate days from lifting, aerobic work at this dose did not measurably blunt strength or muscle gains in trials [@Schumann2021_concurrentMA].

p1-aero.record: Activity and machine, duration, distance or average speed and incline (if shown), and session RPE.
p1-aero.notes: You may replace this with a hike, dance class or martial-arts class of at least the same duration and similar effort.

p1-int.name: Introductory intervals
p1-int.summary: Short hard efforts (1 minute) with 2-minute easy recoveries: your first exposure to high intensity. Bike or rower recommended. Stop at once and follow the [[plan:safety|safety rules]] if you feel chest pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness.

main.rationale: Interval training raises VO₂max a little more than continuous training, especially with longer intervals and more total hard time [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT; @Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]. These short intervals are a stepping stone to the 4 × 4-minute protocol in Phase 2; the bike or rower keeps impact and injury risk low while you are new to hard efforts.

p1-int.record: Machine, number of intervals completed, the resistance or pace used for the hard minutes, and session RPE.

p1-test.name: Reassessment test session
p1-test.summary: Repeat the baseline tests exactly as before: same warm-up, order, time of day and pre-test meal.

items.dose: 1.6 km walk as fast as you can; time and 15-s pulse
Eyes open and closed, each leg

main.rationale: Identical procedures make the comparison with baseline meaningful; changes smaller than each test's measurement error should not be over-interpreted [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability; @Neto2015_AKE_SLR_reliability].

p1-test.record: All results with conditions; compare against baseline in your notes.

p2-ua.name: Upper A (heavier pressing)
p2-ua.summary: Incline press as the main lift, pulldown, then fly + chest-supported row, lateral raise + rear-delt fly, and overhead triceps + incline curl.

main.rationale: Priority muscles for an athletic upper body (upper chest, lateral and rear deltoids, back width, arms) now reach about 12–16 weekly sets, where returns per extra set are still meaningful [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency; @Schoenfeld2017_volume_meta]. Lengthened-position exercises (cable fly, incline curl, overhead triceps extension) are favoured where the evidence supports them [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps; @Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]; machines built muscle as well as free weights in direct comparisons [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], and machine and dumbbell variants are safer alone (practical convention).

p2-ua.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; incline press (3 sets); pulldown (2); superset D (3 rounds); superset E (2 rounds); chest and hamstring stretch.
p2-ua.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set; note the bench angle used for incline work.

p2-la.name: Lower A (squat)
p2-la.summary: Barbell back squat in a rack with safety arms, seated leg curl, leg extension + calf raise, hanging knee raise.

items.warmupSets: 2–3 ramp sets (~50% × 8, ~70% × 4, plus ~85% × 2 once the working load is 60 kg or more; start from the empty bar)
items.note: Safety arms set just below your lowest bar position, every set. Never grind a rep.

main.rationale: Deep squats grew the glutes and adductors more than half squats [@Kubo2019_squatDepth]; a rack with safety arms makes heavy squatting safe without a spotter. Reclining the leg-extension backrest grew the rectus femoris more [@Larsen2025_legExtHipAngle]; standing calf raises target the gastrocnemius [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf]. Leg volume stays moderate (about 10–13 weekly sets) for athletic proportions and to leave capacity for running and hiking.

p2-la.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; squat (3 sets); leg curl (2); hamstring and hip-flexor stretches.
p2-la.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set; safety-arm height in the notes.

p2-ub.name: Upper B (pull-ups and pulling)
p2-ub.summary: Pull-ups first, flat press + row, shoulder press, lateral raise + face pull, pushdown + preacher curl.

items.load: Bodyweight if you can do the rep range; otherwise assisted (machine or band). Add load once all sets reach 8 reps at 2 reps in reserve.

main.rationale: Vertical and horizontal pulls are both included for back width and thickness (anatomical inference; no long-term trial compares them directly). Leading with pull-ups prioritises a skill goal [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta]. One lateral-raise exposure on each upper day plus one on Lower B give the most frequent stimulus to the muscle that most widens the shoulders (inference).

p2-ub.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; pull-ups (3 sets); press + row superset (3 rounds); lateral raise + face pull (2 rounds); stretches.
p2-ub.record: Load (or assistance), reps and RPE per working set.

p2-lb.name: Lower B (hinge and single-leg)
p2-lb.summary: Barbell Romanian deadlift, Bulgarian split squat (left first), leg press, calf press + lateral raise, farmer's carry.

items.warmupSets: 2–3 ramp sets (~50% × 8, ~70% × 4, plus ~85% × 2 once the working load is 60 kg or more; start from the empty bar)

main.rationale: The Romanian deadlift loads the hamstrings and glutes at long lengths and doubles as flexibility training through range; the Bulgarian split squat gives single-leg strength and balance demand for your weaker left side; loaded carries train grip and the trunk muscles (practical convention); trunk-muscle training in general improved strength and power in athletes [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]. The lateral raise here is a third weekly exposure for the lateral deltoid, which recovers quickly from light, high-rep work (inference).

p2-lb.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; RDL (3 sets); split squat (2 per leg); hamstring stretch.
p2-lb.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set; carry load and distance.

p2-hiit.name: 4 × 4 intervals
p2-hiit.summary: Four hard intervals of 4 minutes (3 minutes in weeks 1–3) with 3-minute easy recoveries. Bike, rower or uphill treadmill walking.

main.rationale: The protocol meets the three features most linked to superior VO₂max gains over continuous training: intervals of at least 2 minutes, at least 15 minutes of hard work per session, and programmes lasting weeks [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA; @Helgerud2007_4x4RCT]. On average HIIT adds about 1.4 mL·kg^−1^·min^−1^ over continuous training, with low certainty [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Without a heart-rate monitor, 'hard' means you can say only a few words; heart-rate equations are too imprecise individually (standard error about 11 bpm, so a true maximum can sit about ±20 bpm from the estimate) to rely on [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax; @Scherr2013_RPE].

p2-hiit.record: Machine, resistance or speed/incline in the hard intervals, intervals completed, session RPE.
p2-hiit.notes: If you cannot hold the effort for the last interval, reduce the intensity slightly next time rather than stopping early. Weeks 1–3 use 3-minute intervals. Stop at once and follow the [[plan:safety|safety rules]] if you feel chest pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness.

p2-run.name: Run–walk
p2-run.summary: This week: {{rwText}}. Each run stays within about 10% of your longest run in the previous 30 days.

items.dose: {{rwText}} at an easy running effort (RPE 4–5, short sentences possible); walk briskly between
Then 10 min brisk walking or easy cycling

main.rationale: Novice runners are injured roughly twice as often per hour as experienced runners, and no weekly progression rule (including the '10% rule') has been shown to prevent injuries [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence; @Buist2008_GRONORUN]. The clearest signal is single-session spikes: runs more than 10% longer than the longest run of the previous 30 days were followed by more overuse injuries in a large observational cohort [@Frandsen2025_spikes]. This plan keeps every session within that limit and starts small; a smaller start reduced injuries only in a per-protocol analysis of one small trial in novice runners with obesity [@Bertelsen2018_starttorun]. Run–walk itself is a reasonable but untested method.

p2-run.record: Total running time, distance if known, surface or treadmill, session RPE, and any pain (location, 0–10) during or the next morning.
p2-run.notes: Comfortable, cushioned shoes are a sensible default [@Relph2022_shoesCochrane; @Malisoux2020_cushioning]. If any pain exceeds 3/10 or lingers to the next morning, repeat the previous week's step. A hike, ride or dance class can replace this session occasionally, but repeat the skipped run–walk step afterwards.

p2-test.name: Phase 2 test session
p2-test.summary: 2.4 km run test if you can run 20+ minutes continuously (otherwise repeat the walking test), then the strength, jump, balance and flexibility tests.

items.dose: 2.4 km at the fastest even pace you can sustain (or the 1.6 km walking test)
Eyes open and closed, each leg

main.rationale: Same battery and conditions as before, with the run test replacing the walking test once running is established [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility].

p2-test.record: All results with the conditions; compare against previous tests.

p3-ua.name: Upper A
p3-ua.summary: Main press (Smith incline in Block 1, barbell bench press in Block 2, dumbbell incline in Block 3), vertical pull, chest isolation + row, deltoids, arms.

items.note: In a rack with safety arms at chest height minus ~2 cm. Never to failure.

items.load: Bodyweight or assisted; add load at 3 × 10.

main.rationale: Block-wise rotation of the main press and some accessories adds planned variety, which supports motivation and can broaden hypertrophy across a muscle, while anchor lifts stay constant within a block so progress is measurable [@Kassiano2022_variationSR; @Fonseca2014_exerciseVariation]. The heavier Block 2 targets maximal strength, which responds best to heavier loads [@Lopez2021_load_NMA].

p3-ua.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; main press (3 sets); vertical pull (2); superset D (3 rounds); stretches.
p3-ua.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

p3-la.name: Lower A (squat)
p3-la.summary: Back squat (heavier in Block 2), seated leg curl, leg extension + calf raise, core. Jumps or agility in the warm-up from week 9.

main.rationale: The squat remains the anchor lower-body lift; heavier work in Block 2 improves maximal strength specifically [@Lopez2021_load_NMA]. Jumps before lifting train power and reactive strength when you are fresh [@Markovic2007_vertjump; @RamirezCampillo2023_RSI].

p3-la.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; squat (3 sets); leg curl (2); stretches.
p3-la.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set; jump contacts done.

p3-ub.name: Upper B
p3-ub.summary: Pull-ups (weighted when ready), dumbbell or machine press + row, shoulder press, lateral raise + face pull, arms.

items.load: Add load (belt or dumbbell between the feet) once all sets reach the top of the range at 2 reps in reserve; use assistance otherwise.

main.rationale: Weighted pull-ups give a progressive, measurable back-width lift that also builds the strength you want for climbing, martial arts and daily tasks. Equipment variety (machine press, one-arm row, hammer curl) adds novelty without changing the muscles trained [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta; @BazValle2019_variationMotivation].

p3-ub.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; pull-ups (3 sets); press + row (2 rounds); lateral raise + face pull (3 rounds); stretches.
p3-ub.record: Load (added or assisted), reps and RPE per working set.

p3-lb.name: Lower B (hinge and single-leg)
p3-lb.summary: Romanian deadlift (trap-bar deadlift in Block 2), reverse lunge, hip thrust or leg press, calf press + lateral raise, carries.

items.note: Stop each set with 2–3 reps in reserve; reset between reps.

main.rationale: The trap-bar deadlift is a heavy whole-body pull that is easier to learn and to bail from than the conventional deadlift, suiting a strength block when training alone (practical inference). Hip thrusts produced similar glute growth to squats, so they are an optional variant rather than a necessity [@Plotkin2023_hipThrustVsSquat].

p3-lb.shortVersion: ≈40 min: warm-up; main hinge (3 sets); lunge (2 per leg); stretches.
p3-lb.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

p3-hiit.name: Intervals
p3-hiit.summary: {{intText}}. Running now allowed if your run progression went well; otherwise bike or rower.

main.rationale: Long intervals with plenty of total hard time drive VO₂max [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA; @Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Block 2's 2-minute intervals are harder but shorter, adding variety while still meeting the ≥2-minute criterion. All-out sprint intervals are not used: in two small trials in well-trained young runners, all-out treadmill sprints caused 8 injuries in one (none with 4 × 4) and raised VO₂max less than 4 × 4 in both [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT; @Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT].

p3-hiit.record: Machine or run, pace or resistance during work intervals, intervals completed, session RPE.

p3-long.name: Long session (run, hike, ride or class)
p3-long.summary: {{longMin}} minutes easy: continuous running, a hike, a ride, or a dance or martial-arts class.

items.dose: {{longMin}} min at RPE 3–4 (or a class of similar length)

main.rationale: Extra aerobic volume adds to fat loss: in trials in adults with overweight, each additional 30 minutes per week reduced waist by about 0.6 cm [@Jayedi2024_aerobicWeightLossDoseResponse]; keeping it easy limits the recovery cost (inference). Enjoyable skill-based options count: dance improved fitness at least as much as other exercise [@FongYan2018_danceMA], and learning a structured skill is the most plausible route to the coordination you want, because coordination and agility gains are task-specific [@Kummel2016_specificity; @NygaardFalch2019_COD]. If running, keep any run within 10% of your longest run in the previous 30 days [@Frandsen2025_spikes].

p3-long.record: Activity, duration, distance or elevation if known, session RPE.
p3-long.notes: Hiking with elevation gain, a dance class or a martial-arts class are all good substitutes when they are enjoyable and last about as long.

p3-test.name: Test session
p3-test.summary: 2.4 km run, push-ups, pull-ups, broad jump, balance and flexibility, under identical conditions to previous tests.

items.dose: Eyes open and closed, each leg

main.rationale: Standardised repeat testing [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility; @Powden2015_WBLT_reliability].

p4-ua.name: Upper A
p4-ua.summary: Your chosen main press, vertical pull, chest isolation + row, deltoids, arms. Swap variants each cycle from the alternatives on each exercise page.

items.note: Or another press from its alternatives list.

main.rationale: Same evidence base as Phases 2–3; in continuation cycles you set the weekly sets for each muscle by your emphasis (12–16 for priorities, 6–8 to maintain) [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency; @Spiering2021_minimalDose].

p4-ua.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

p4-la.name: Lower A (squat)
p4-la.summary: Squat variant, leg curl, leg extension + calf raise, core.

items.note: Or hack squat / leg press as the main lift for a cycle.

main.rationale: As in Phases 2–3 [@Kubo2019_squatDepth; @Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl].

p4-la.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

p4-ub.name: Upper B
p4-ub.summary: Pull-ups, press + row, shoulder press, lateral raise + face pull, arms.

main.rationale: As in Phases 2–3 [@Nunes2021_exerciseOrderMeta; @Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].

p4-ub.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

p4-lb.name: Lower B (hinge and single-leg)
p4-lb.summary: Romanian deadlift, Bulgarian split squat, leg press, calf press + lateral raise, carries.

main.rationale: As in Phases 2–3; the athletic warm-up keeps jumps and agility in the week [@Markovic2007_vertjump].

p4-lb.record: Load, reps and RPE per working set.

pm-a.name: Maintenance full body A
pm-a.summary: One hard set or two per pattern: squat, press, pull, hinge, plus lateral raises.

main.rationale: About one-third of usual volume at the usual effort maintains strength and muscle for weeks to months [@Spiering2021_minimalDose; @Bickel2011_maintenanceDose].

pm-b.name: Maintenance full body B
pm-b.summary: Pull-ups, flat press + row, split squat, lateral raise.

main.rationale: As session A [@Spiering2021_minimalDose; @Iversen2021_time_efficient].
Keeping intensity high preserves VO₂max even when frequency and duration fall [@Spiering2021_minimalDose].

pm-steady.name: Maintenance steady session
pm-steady.summary: {{z2min}} minutes at a conversational effort, or a hike or class.

main.rationale: Easy aerobic volume counts towards the 150–300 weekly minutes of moderate activity recommended for health [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines].

pa-a.name: Away full body A
pa-a.summary: Bulgarian split squat, push-up + row, single-leg Romanian deadlift + pike push-up, lateral raise + calf raise, then reverse crunches. Use the hardest rung that still gives the target reps with control, and end sets close to failure: effort replaces load.

items.warmupSets: 1 easier set × 8 per side (rear foot on the floor)
items.load: Bodyweight, rear foot on a chair, sofa or bed edge. Next rungs: a 3–4 s lowering with a 1 s pause at the bottom, then a loaded backpack hugged to your chest.
items.note: Left leg first; match its reps on the right.

items.load: Your ladder rung: hands on a table, bed or stairs → floor → feet on a chair → backpack on. Use the rung that gives 6–20 reps at the target effort.
Overhand grip on the edge of a sturdy table, lying underneath it; test the table first (see the exercise page). No safe table: [[ex:backpack-row]], each arm.
Bodyweight, then a loaded backpack held in the hand opposite the standing leg. Fingertips on a wall or chair at first.
The rung that gives 5–15 controlled reps: hands on a step or bed edge, then the floor, then feet on a chair.
Two filled 1–2 L bottles, or one loaded bag one arm at a time; a band if you have one.
One leg at a time, the ball of the foot on a stair edge or a sturdy step and a hand on the wall; when both sets reach 20 reps at the target effort, wear a loaded backpack.
Bent knees first; then a 3–4 s lowering, then straighter legs, then an incline holding a bed frame or heavy sofa.

main.rationale:
**Selection.** The session covers a squat pattern, an upper-body push and an upper-body pull, the core of a time-efficient programme [@Iversen2021_time_efficient], plus a hinge, an overhead push, the lateral deltoids and the calves, each in the hardest bodyweight version you can control.
- *Bulgarian split squat:* putting most of your weight on one leg makes body weight a real load (biomechanical reasoning). In 18 young rugby players, training only the (loaded) rear-foot-elevated split squat raised back-squat [[term:1rm|1RM]] as much as back-squat training [@Speirs2016_RFESSvsBackSquat], and unilateral and bilateral training gave similar early gains in squat strength and power in 38 untrained adults [@McCurdy2005_uniVsBiUntrained].
- *Push-up:* taken to failure, push-ups grew the chest (+18.3%) and triceps (+9.5%) about as much as a bench press at a matched light load in a small 8-week trial [@Kikuchi2017_pushupVsBench]. A floor push-up loads about 64–66% of body weight, raising the feet makes it heavier and raising the hands lighter (force-plate studies) [@Gouvali2005_pushupVariantsGRF; @Ebben2011_pushupKinetics]; the ladder uses exactly that.
- *Inverted row:* probably the best pull available without a bar (inference). In 7 men it produced the highest latissimus and upper-back activation and the lowest lumbar load of three rows (EMG and modelling) [@Fenwick2009_invertedRowSpine], and near horizontal it put about 69–73% of body weight through the arms of 12 trained athletes on suspension straps [@Vural2023_suspensionLoadBW].
- *Single-leg Romanian deadlift:* hamstrings and glutes at long length. In a small trial of 20 active adults supervised remotely by video, it improved a hamstring endurance test (the single-leg hamstring bridge) as much as Nordic curls, but the single-leg RDL group needed added load (median 7.5 kg) [@Behan2024_NHEvsSLRDLremote], hence the backpack rung.
- *Pike push-up:* the nearest substitute for an overhead press; with the hips high, the arms push close to vertically and the hands carry more of your weight as the feet come closer (biomechanical reasoning).
- *Lateral raise:* the only exercise here that trains the lateral deltoids directly. Dumbbell and cable raises grew the muscle equally in 24 trained adults [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable], and at matched effort elastic tubing produced deltoid activation similar to dumbbells (EMG in 16 women with neck and shoulder pain) [@Andersen2010_dumbbellVsTubingEMG], so bottles, a bag or a band should serve (inference).
- *Single-leg calf raise:* standing raises grew the gastrocnemius far more than seated ones in a small trial in 14 untrained adults [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf], and the pause in the stretch follows a trial in 42 untrained women in which partial reps in the stretched position grew it most [@Kassiano2023_calfLP]; that a pause does the same is inference.

**Dose.** The rep ranges are wide (6–20, 8–20, 15–30) because bodyweight rungs change the load in big steps; light, moderate and heavy loads built similar muscle when sets went to failure [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], and sets of 20–25 reps matched sets of 8–12 in trained men [@Morton2016_20to25repsTrained]. Across sessions A and B this gives about 5–9 hard sets a week for most muscles (calves and biceps get less), counting sets for helper muscles as half [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency], probably a maintenance dose for Phases 2–4 (inference; see [[phase:pa|Away mode]]). Rests of 45–75 s within supersets keep the session to 55 minutes. Growth benefited slightly from resting more than 60 s but not appreciably beyond about 90 s [@Singer2024_rest_meta]; in a superset each muscle also rests while you do the paired exercise, so its own sets are well over 90 s apart. Supersets of non-competing muscles matched traditional sets for gains [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].

**Effort.** With light loads, effort matters most: in 25 untrained men, knee-extension sets at 30% of 1RM grew the quadriceps 7.8% when taken to failure and only 2.8% (not significant) when stopped short [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load], and light loads taken to failure recruited type II fibres too (a mechanistic study) [@Morton2019_fibre_activation]. So from week 2, Away sets end 0–2 reps from failure, closer than your gym free-weight sets, and the last set of push-ups, rows and split squats may reach failure: with no bar to get stuck under, that is safe (practical convention). Effort estimates were less accurate in sets of more than 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], one more reason to move up a rung rather than let sets grow very long.

pa-a.shortVersion: Short on time (≈25 min)? March on the spot for 3 min, then do the scapular push-ups and paused squats from the warm-up; 2 sets of the split squat (left first); 2 rounds of the push-up + row superset; 2 rounds of the lateral raise + calf raise superset; finish with the hamstring stretch. Keep this week's effort targets.
pa-a.record: In Hevy (routine 'Away A'), log each exercise under its Away name ([[plan:logging]]): the new ones by their 'Log as' names ('Inverted Row' or 'Backpack Row', 'Pike Pushup', 'Reverse Crunch') and the gym ones as custom '(Away)' copies ('Bulgarian Split Squat (Away)', 'Push Up (Away)', 'Single Leg Romanian Deadlift (Away)', 'Lateral Raise (Away)', 'Standing Calf Raise (Away)'); the exercise cards above show the same names. Record reps and RPE for every working set, with the rung in the exercise note (e.g. 'feet on chair', 'table row, knees bent'). A backpack or bottle load goes in the weight field in kg: weigh it on your scale (your weight holding it minus your weight without it). Log the split squat, single-leg RDL and calf raise for the left and right leg, and any pain (site, 0–10).
pa-a.notes: No sturdy table? Do [[ex:backpack-row]] for the row. A long loop band, if you have one, can load the lateral raises and rows; see each exercise's notes for training without equipment. Any gym nearby beats all of this: use it, swapping exercises as needed ([[rule:substitution]]).

pa-b.name: Away full body B
pa-b.summary: Nordic curls first, then reverse lunges, push-up + row (a harder rung and, on a bar, a new grip), triceps extension + lateral raise, and side planks.

items.load: Heels hooked under a heavy sofa or bed that cannot tip or slide (test it with a hard pull), or held by a person; knees on a folded towel. Lower as slowly as you can and catch yourself with your hands.
items.note: Every rep is a maximal effort to slow the fall, so the rep count, not reps in reserve, sets the dose. Week 1: 2 × 3–5 only (the app shows 2 sets that week), however easy they feel; from week 2, 3 × 3–8, ending a set at 8 or sooner when your break point comes clearly earlier than on the first rep. No safe anchor: [[ex:sliding-leg-curl]] in its place, 2 × 6–10 (eccentric-only, both legs) at 2–3 RIR in week 1, then 3 × 6–15 at 1–2 RIR.

items.load: Bodyweight. Next rungs: front foot on a stair or a thick book (a deficit, so you sink deeper), then a loaded backpack.
Today a harder variant than session A if you can: feet on a chair, or hands on two stacks of books for a deficit. Otherwise A's rung with a 3 s lowering.

On a bar, rings or straps: an underhand grip (palms towards you) to involve the biceps more (anatomical reasoning). Under a table, which allows only an overhand grip, keep A's grip and slow the lowering to 3–4 s, or do the [[ex:backpack-row]] with your palm turned forward.
Hands on a kitchen counter or sturdy table edge, body straight; a lower surface or feet further back makes it harder.
As in session A: bottles, a loaded bag one arm at a time, or a band.
From the knees until 20 s on the feet is possible; beyond 45 s, raise the top leg or rest a loaded bag on your hip.

main.rationale:
**Selection.**
- *Nordic curl first,* while you are fresh: it is the hardest and most technical exercise here, and the only way to load knee flexion heavily without a machine (biomechanical reasoning). Low volumes work: in a meta-analysis of 13 studies, mostly in athletes and active young adults, low- and high-volume programmes of 6 weeks or more gave similarly large gains in [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] strength (g 2.28 vs 2.12), and biceps femoris fascicles (fibre bundles) lengthened [@Cuthbert2020_NHEvolumeMeta]; in 45 trained young men, gains were then maintained on as little as 4 reps a week, with weight added once they could control the descent [@Miura2025_NHEultralowMaintenance]. In 44 adults with tight hamstrings, low-volume Nordic curls improved passive knee extension as much as static stretching (6.1° vs 5.1° more than controls) [@Henderson2025_NHEvsStaticStretch], which should suit your toe-touch limitation (inference), and in athletes, programmes that included them roughly halved hamstring injuries (risk ratio 0.49) [@vanDyk2019_NHEinjuryMeta].
- *Reverse lunge:* the week's second single-leg knee exercise, with a different stance from the split squat; the deficit rung adds range (practical convention). [[term:unilateral|Unilateral]] training built muscle like bilateral training (very imprecise evidence) and improved single-leg strength most [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta].
- *Push-up and row, varied:* a harder push-up rung and an underhand row grip (on a bar, rings or straps; under a table, a slower lowering instead) load the same muscles a little differently. In a review of 8 small studies in young men, deliberate, reasoned variation could help regional growth, whereas excessive, random rotation may blunt gains [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. The underhand grip lets the biceps, also a forearm supinator, pull in its strongest position (anatomical reasoning); in an EMG study, biceps activation was very high with either grip [@Youdas2016_invertedRowEMG].
- *Bodyweight triceps extension:* direct triceps work alongside the presses. With the arms raised in front of the head, the long head works at a longer length than in a pushdown (anatomical reasoning); in 21 untrained adults, overhead cable extensions grew the triceps about 1.4–1.5 times more than neutral-arm ones [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps], but whether this exercise gets the same benefit is inference.
- *Side plank:* lateral trunk work with no equipment. Trunk muscle training improved strength and local muscular endurance in athletes [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta], though abdominal exercises alone did not reduce waist size or abdominal fat in a small trial [@Vispute2011_absSpot].

**Dose and effort.** As in session A [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load; @Pelland2025_volume_frequency], with one exception: Nordic curls stay low-rep and every rep stays under control. A first session of 24 reps reduced eccentric strength for up to 3 days and raised soreness on days 2–3 in 13 trained men [@Coratella2025_NHEmuscleDamageRBE], and in untrained people a single earlier bout of eccentric exercise cut later soreness and strength loss, most when done 2–4 days before [@Boyd2023_preconditioningEIMDmeta]; hence the small dose in week 1 (inference). A dose meta-regression found no link between Nordic volume and strength gain and suggested about 29–64 reps a week after a progressive start [@Franke2025_NHEdoseMetaRegression]; from week 2 this session gives 9–24 reps, so 9–48 a week depending on how many B sessions the week holds.

pa-b.shortVersion: Short on time (≈25 min)? March on the spot for 3 min, then the scapular push-ups, paused squats and glute bridges from the warm-up; 2 easy partial-range Nordic reps, then 2 sets of Nordic curls; 2 sets of reverse lunges per side (left first); 2 rounds of the push-up + row superset; 2 rounds of the triceps extension + lateral raise superset; hamstring stretch. Keep this week's effort targets.
pa-b.record: In Hevy (routine 'Away B'), log each exercise under its Away name ([[plan:logging]]): the new ones by their 'Log as' names ('Nordic Hamstrings Curls' or 'Sliding Leg Curl', 'Inverted Row' or 'Backpack Row', 'Triceps Extension (Bodyweight)') and the gym ones as custom '(Away)' copies ('Reverse Lunge (Away)', 'Push Up (Away)', 'Lateral Raise (Away)', 'Side Plank (Away)'); the exercise cards above show the same names. Nordic curls as reps per set, with how far down you controlled the descent in the note (e.g. 'controlled to halfway'); reverse-lunge reps for each leg; push-up and row rung and reps; lateral-raise load in kg and reps; side-plank seconds per side. RPE for every working set except the Nordic curls, and any pain (site, 0–10).
pa-b.notes: Nordic curls need an anchor that cannot move: test the sofa or bed with a hard pull before the first rep, pad your knees, and keep your hands ready to catch you. Expect sore hamstrings for 2–3 days after the first session; it is much milder after later ones.

pa-steady.name: Away steady session
pa-steady.summary: {{z2min}} minutes of brisk walking at a conversational effort, on hills or stairs if you have them, or a hike, swim, ride or class of similar length.

items.dose: {{z2min}} min at RPE 3–4 (full sentences): brisk walk (hills or stairs if you have them), or easy running only if your current phase already includes running

main.rationale: In a meta-analysis of 28 studies in healthy adults aged 18–45, continuous endurance training raised VO₂max by about 4.9 mL/kg/min versus no exercise [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA]. Brisk walking, uphill where you can, is the easiest way to train continuously anywhere (practical convention), although it may be gentler than the training in those trials (inference). The [[term:talk-test|talk test]] needs no equipment: comfortable speech is possible below the [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold]] and becomes difficult close to it [@Persinger2004_talkTest; @ReedPipe2014_talkTestReview]. Running stays out unless your phase already includes it, because novice runners were injured about twice as often per hour of running as recreational runners [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence]. The session also counts towards the 150–300 weekly minutes of moderate activity recommended for health [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines].

pa-steady.record: Activity, duration, distance or route if your phone records it, and session RPE; note hills, flights of stairs or a backpack load if you used them.
pa-steady.notes: A hike, dance or martial-arts class, swim or cycle ride of similar duration counts.

pa-int.name: Away intervals
pa-int.summary: {{intText}} on stairs, a hill or, if your phase already includes running, a run; a low-impact bodyweight circuit if you have none of these. If your gym phase has no intervals yet, do a second steady session instead (see the notes below). Stop at once and follow the [[plan:safety|safety rules]] if you feel chest pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness.

main.rationale: This keeps the role of your gym interval session, a weekly dose of hard aerobic work, because intensity is what maintained endurance when training was cut back [@Spiering2021_minimalDose]. Stairs or a hill come first: bodyweight-only [[term:hiit|HIIT]] improved cardiorespiratory fitness versus no exercise ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.75) but less than running or cycling training (SMD −0.40) in pooled trials [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta], whereas ~2-min stair ascents raised [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] by 17.1% relative to controls in one small trial in sedentary young women [@Boreham2005_stairClimbing]. Two-minute efforts fall within the longer-interval (≥2 min) format linked to larger VO₂max gains [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA] and fit an ordinary stairwell or hill (practical convention). The session totals 8–12 min of hard work rather than a 4-min 'Tabata', because very short bodyweight protocols often failed to raise VO₂max [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta] and, in one trial, kept no benefit at 2 months [@Islam2019_TabataVsVICT]. Jumping moves wait until Phase 2, as the programme adds impact gradually (practical convention).

pa-int.record: Mode (stairs, hill, run or circuit), efforts completed, floors or distance per effort if you can count them, and session RPE; in Hevy, a cardio entry with the duration and these details in the note.
pa-int.notes: Match your gym phase: if it has no interval session yet (Phase 0, or Phase 1 before week 7), skip the pick-ups and walk briskly for {{z2min}} min at RPE 3–4 instead, as in the steady session ([[ex:cardio-steady]]); in the rest of Phase 1, keep the hard efforts at RPE 7–8, as in your gym intervals (practical convention). With only a few floors, climb and turn back down continuously and push only on the way up; in one small uncontrolled trial in sedentary young women, 60-s efforts up and down a single flight still raised VO₂peak by 7% over 6 weeks [@Allison2017_stairSprintSIT]. A bike ride or swim with hard 2-min efforts also works (practical convention).
